title: They thought his story ended in betrayal.
paragraphs: They thought his story ended in betrayal.
They thought the pit was the final chapter.
They thought slavery erased the promise.
The room was quiet in a way that feels heavy. Not peaceful. Not calm. The kind of silence that presses against your chest. The kind that comes when a life is reaching its final breath.
Joseph lay there, no longer the young dreamer with stars bowing before him, no longer the forgotten prisoner, no longer the second ruler of Egypt feared and respected.
Now… just a man. A dying man.
Genesis 50:24 records something that sounds simple, but carries eternity inside it:

“אָנֹכִי מֵת; וֵאלֹהִים פָּקֹד יִפְקֹד אֶתְכֶם”
(Anokhi met; ve’Elohim pakod yifkod etchem)
“I am dying, but God will surely visit you.”
Joseph wasn’t clinging to life. He wasn’t bargaining for more time. He wasn’t rehearsing regrets or defending his story.
Because a life surrendered to God doesn’t end in fear… it ends in faith.

He could have said, “I was betrayed.”
He could have said, “My brothers ruined my life.”
He could have said, “I deserved better.”
But instead, years earlier, Joseph already rewrote his own pain with truth:

“אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה; אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה”
(Atem chashavtem alai ra’ah; Elohim chashavah le’tovah)
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” (Genesis 50:20)
That truth will either offend you… or free you.
Because it means your story—yes, the parts you hide, the parts you’re ashamed of, the parts that still sting—are not wasted pages.
They are ink in God’s hands.
Joseph understood something many believers still wrestle with:
God doesn’t just work around your pain.
The Hebrew word “חָשַׁב” (chashav) means to weave, to plan, to account with intention.
He didn’t build monuments to his success.
“God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.” (Genesis 50:25)
Even when it looked like blessing.
Even when it felt like promotion.
Even when everything finally worked out.
Joseph knew this world—this system, this temporary comfort—was not the promise.
He was waiting for something greater.
The Hebrew repeats it for emphasis: “פָּקֹד יִפְקֹד” (pakod yifkod) — “God will surely visit.”
And here’s where it gets personal.
Because some of you are in your “pit” season right now.
Some of you are living in the “false accusation” chapter.
Some of you feel like God forgot you in a prison nobody else can see.
Joseph’s last words answer you across generations:
Even when you don’t understand the plot.
Even when the chapter feels too dark to keep reading.
Even when the silence feels louder than His voice.
The Greek New Testament later echoes this same heartbeat in a different voice, a different time, but the same Spirit:

“πάντα συνεργεῖ εἰς ἀγαθόν”
(panta synergei eis agathon)
The mistakes you wish you could undo.
Because Jesus doesn’t edit your story.
But that Christ entered your brokenness and rewrote your ending.
Joseph descended into a pit and rose to save nations.
Jesus descended into death and rose to save eternity.
And just like Joseph’s story didn’t end in the pit…
Yours doesn’t end in your failure.
This is where grace becomes more than a word.
It becomes the moment you stop pretending you’re okay.
It becomes the moment you finally whisper, “I need Jesus.”
This hit something you’ve been avoiding, didn’t it?
And moments like this are where eternity shifts.
Because this is what we do here—we don’t perform religion.
We walk through real stories, real pain, real redemption.
And if you’re ready to go deeper—truly deeper into Scripture, healing, discipleship, and transformation—there’s something waiting for you.
If this message stirred something in you, don’t just feel it—act on it.
Supporting this mission, sharing truth, and helping others encounter Jesus is one way you can glorify God with what you’ve been given.
Because someone else is still in their pit… and your share might be the rope God uses to pull them out.
Joseph died with a promise on his lips.
And that promise is still alive in you.
And the ending… will look nothing like the beginning.
